Evolution of WHO HCV Guidelines Toward Simplified Service Delivery The WHO guidelines emphasize decentralization, integration, and task-shifting to improve access to hepatitis C virus (HCV) testing and treatment. These strategies aim to move care out of specialty clinics and into community-based settings. Decentralization: HCV testing and treatment should be delivered at peripheral health or community-based facilities, ideally at the same site, to enhance access to diagnosis, care, and treatment. These facilities may include primary care centers, harm reduction sites, prisons, HIV/ART clinics, community-based organizations, and outreach services. Integration: HCV testing and treatment should be integrated with existing care services at peripheral health facilities, such as primary care, harm reduction programs (e.g., needle and syringe programs, opioid agonist maintenance therapy), prisons, and HIV/ART services. Task-Sharing: HCV testing, care, and treatment can be delivered by trained non-specialist doctors and nurses to expand access. This approach is supported by strong recommendations and moderate certainty of evidence. Rationale for Decentralization, Integration, and Task-Sharing A review of 142 studies from 33 countries demonstrated that full decentralization and integration significantly increased the uptake of HCV viral load testing, linkage to care, and treatment, particularly among people who inject drugs (PWID) and prisoners. Cure rates (SVR12) were comparable between specialists and non-specialists across all populations and settings. Surveys and interviews highlighted strong support for decentralized and integrated services, emphasizing the importance of non-judgmental and non-stigmatizing approaches, especially for PWID and people living with HIV (PLHIV). Implementation Considerations Service delivery recommendations should be adapted to different contexts, countries, and populations. Implementation should align with principles of simplified service delivery, such as standardized algorithms, differentiated care strategies, community engagement, peer support, efficient procurement, supply management, and data systems. Effective planning and coordination are required, including integrated data systems and cross-training of healthcare providers. Decentralization may not be suitable for all settings or clients and could be inefficient in high-income countries (HICs) with low infection burdens. Advances in HCV Testing and Diagnostics Testing Recommendations (2017): Focused testing for high-risk populations, individuals with clinical suspicion of chronic viral hepatitis, family members, and healthcare workers. General population testing in settings with ≥2% or ≥5% HBsAg or HCV antibody prevalence. Testing Methods: A single serological assay (EIA or RDT) meeting performance standards, followed by prompt NAT testing and linkage to care. Confirmation of HCV viraemia using lab-based NAT (RNA) or core antigen assays with comparable sensitivity. Promoting Uptake and Linkage: Use of dried blood spot (DBS) specimens for virology and serology. On-site or immediate RDT testing with same-day results. Trained peer and lay health workers. Clinician reminders to prompt provider-initiated testing. Integration of testing within a single facility. Point-of-Care (POC) HCV RNA Testing (2022): POC HCV RNA assays can serve as an alternative to lab-based NAT assays for diagnosing HCV viraemia and as a test of cure. Reflex HCV RNA testing is recommended for individuals with positive HCV antibody results to promote linkage to care and treatment. Treatment Recommendations for Adolescents and Children Treatment of HCV-infected adolescents and older children is highly effective and safe, with SVR12 rates ≥95% across all age groups for regimens such as SOF/DCV, G/P, and SOF/VEL. Serious adverse events and treatment discontinuations are rare. Early treatment in childhood and adolescence prevents disease progression, liver damage, and stigma while reducing transmission risks. Key Approvals: DAA regimens (SOF/VEL, G/P, SOF/LED) are approved for use in children as young as three years old. Challenges: Limited data on younger children (3–5 years) and very low certainty of evidence for all regimens in this age group. Extrapolation from pharmacokinetic modeling in adolescents suggests appropriate dosing for children based on weight. Implementation Considerations for Pediatric Treatment National plans and guidelines should include case-finding, testing, care, and treatment for children and adolescents. Resources should ensure the availability of generic products, pediatric formulations, and cost reductions. Adolescent-friendly services should address vulnerable populations and consent issues for testing. Community and Healthcare Worker Perspectives Surveys indicate strong preferences for community-based, integrated services that offer testing and treatment at the same site. Respondents emphasized the importance of convenience, continuity of care, and rapid initiation of treatment. Healthcare workers also expressed a preference for treating all children aged three years and older, with a trend toward prioritizing older age groups.
